questions.q: What is an endowment, according to the summary?
a: A donation an institution keeps rather than sells
A loan that must be repaid with interest
A fund that has to be spent within a year
A fee charged for managing institutional money
questions.why: Lesson 1 defines an endowment as a donation the organization must keep under its ownership for as long as it operates.

questions.q: Why do some institutions hesitate to accept endowments?
a: Donors may attach conditions on how the money is used
Endowments tend to lower an institution's credit rating
Endowments have to be paid back once profits arrive
Endowments are taxed more heavily than normal income
questions.why: Lesson 1 says donors may demand certain research, spending choices or decisions that executives dislike.

questions.q: What are the three core aspects of investment analysis?
a: Asset allocation, market timing and security selection
Risk tolerance, liquidity and tax planning
Diversification, rebalancing and cost control
Research, valuation and portfolio review
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists asset allocation, market timing and security selection as the starting points of analysis.

questions.q: Which of those aspects matters most for predicting returns?
a: Asset allocation
Market timing
Security selection
Portfolio rebalancing
questions.why: Lesson 2 says asset allocation is the most important factor when forecasting returns.

questions.q: Why should no single asset class exceed roughly 25 to 30 percent of a portfolio?
a: A crash could leave too much of your net worth stuck
Smaller holdings always produce higher average returns
Regulators cap how much one class may be held
Fees rise sharply once a holding passes that size
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns that concentrating more than that leaves too much of your net value blocked in a crash.
